catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-1-q1.explanation: B - saveTo save face is a set phrase that means ‘to save one’s dignity’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-1-q2.explanation: D - rather thanDo something rather than do something else. The other three phrases are normally used with -ing form (e.g. instead of upsetting them).

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-1-q3.explanation: B - embarkThe only verb that collocates with on. To embark on(upon) something means to commence, to start doing it.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-1-q4.explanation: A - backedTo back up means to support, to reinforce (e.g. to back up your argument with scientific data)

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-1-q5.explanation: D - tellingTo tell lies is the commonly used phrase.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-1-q6.explanation: A - goTo go ahead — to continue, to carry on. Another set phrase.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-1-q7.explanation: B - obviouslyIt fits in the context and it is the only adverb that would require a comma after it in this position of an introductory word.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-1-q8.explanation: B - homeHome truths (usually plural) are unpleasant facts that are told to a person you know well (e.g. you tell your best friend about his bad breath). This is a set phrase.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-2-q9.explanation: howThe more we “invest” in happiness the more happier we become.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-2-q10.explanation: intoTo put time and effort into something. Effort has to be used with ‘into’, but time can have both ‘into’ and ‘in’. Since the preposition is used with both words in this case, you will have to use the only common preposition ‘into’. Using ‘in’ will be regarded as a mistake.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-2-q11.explanation: canNot ‘could’ and not ‘may’ because the fact was actually demonstrated, as it is explained in the sentence that follows.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-2-q12.explanation: theirThe sentence mentions the brains of people who practised meditation.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-2-q13.explanation: inTo keep in check means to keep under control.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-2-q14.explanation: notThe second part of the sentence refutes (proves wrong) the statement made in the previous sentence.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-2-q15.explanation: wayThe way we do something = how we do it.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-2-q16.explanation: makeTo make a difference = to have an effect, to change something.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-3-q17.explanation: indisputableThe context makes it clear that the word has to have negative prefix. The meaning of the word is “beyond doubt, not open to question”. Mind the spelling and use the right negative prefix. If it is not clear whether to use negative prefix or not, try skipping this word and finishing the rest of the sentence to understand it better.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-3-q18.explanation: rigorousHarsh, accurate and very strict. Do not omit ‘u’ at the end as you are supposed to stick to BrE spelling.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-3-q19.explanation: dedicationA noun is needed here. Note the preposition ‘to‘ used with ‘dedication‘.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-3-q20.explanation: enduranceEndurance athletes are required to display both strength and stamina.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-3-q21.explanation: musicalitySensitivity to music or being musical. This can involve feeling the rhythm that dancers need so much.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-3-q22.explanation: dissimilarDouble negative should be used here (not dissimilar = similar) — the authors compare a dance with a football game and it is clear from context that they are alike. Make sure you use the correct negative prefix.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-3-q23.explanation: explosiveIt is important not to be mistaken and use ‘exploding’. The energy the dancer needs is explosive in its nature (comes suddenly, in quick bursts). The energy does not explode.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-3-q24.explanation: repetitiveThe word routine implies that it repeats over and over again — so it is repetitive.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-4-q25.answer: had not/never faced a bigger/such a big
catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-4-q25.explanation: had not/never faced a bigger/such a bigIt is important to understand why we use Past Perfect here. ‘To date’ indicates that the period is finished.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-4-q26.answer: regret not trying harder/regret not having tried harder
catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-4-q26.explanation: regret not trying harder/regret not having tried harderRegret doing/not doing something. Regret is normally used with -ing form.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-4-q27.explanation: gets on my nerves whenUptight means tense or nervous. To get on somebody’s nerves means to upset, unnerve or irritate somebody.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-4-q28.explanation: to make his markTo make one’s mark means to succeed or to become recognised.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-4-q29.explanation: to make dreams come trueDreams come true is an established collocation.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-4-q30.explanation: would rather not takeWould rather not do something indicates lack of desire to do it.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-5-q31.explanation: DAnswers A, B and C are all opinions the rest of the family had about author’s father strange habit. Answer D is what the author thinks of his father, stated in the very first sentence: “a hoarder”. See vocabulary for more information.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-5-q32.explanation: CParagraph 2, second sentence mentions author’s father’s ‘relatively benign symptoms’. What this means is that father’s condition wasn’t as bad as in comparison to those people in the documentary.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-5-q33.explanation: AThe main clue is the mentioned ‘Freudian analysts’. As you know, Freud was a famous psychologist. Evidently Jasmine tried to offset the psychological damage caused by her troubled childhood by choosing an occupation that involves the opposite environment to that witnessed back home.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-5-q34.explanation: DBeginning of paragraph 4 goes: “Jasmine coaxed and cajoled Vasoulla to jettison at least some of her junk”. The less known vocabulary contains the answer here. In short, Jasmine tried to persuade Vasoulla to let go of the things she amassed. Refer to vocabulary for more information. Answers A and B are not mentioned. Answer C is not correct — Vasoulla’s condition did not need to be diagnosed, Jasmine asked the doctor for more information about the illness.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-5-q35.explanation: CEnding of paragraph five: “But she (Vasoulla) was touchingly appreciative of what Jasmine had done for her”. Answer A is wrong — it is clearly stated that Vasoulla was far from completely recovering from her condition. Answer B is not mentioned. Answer D is only a minor detail (“it’s good to see the table again”).

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-5-q36.explanation: BThe whole paragraph talks about how their father is very frugal and afraid that even the slightest part of what he has goes to waste.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-6-q37.explanation: ABlogger A questions “more practical” things about preparing, namely the benefit of learning your lines.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-6-q38.explanation: CBoth bloggers believe that actor himself can’t tell how well he performs. Blogger A: ” actors are not necessarily the best judge of their own performance”, Blogger C: “the actors is simply playing a part, and how well he or she does that is for others to judge”

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-6-q39.explanation: Bloggers B, C and D all focus on the impact that the actor’s performance has on the audience. Blogger A however focuses primarily on technique, preparation, and training from drama school (learning lines, using emotional memory, applying practical techniques). The success of a performance is linked more to technical preparation and the actor’s craft rather than the audience’s reaction to it.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-6-q40.explanation: DBlogger B believes that the best thing is to change somebody’s view on things: “the best part of an actor’s job is to convey that and change the way people think about it”; Blogger D concurs in the very last sentence of his paragraph.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-7-q41.explanation: GThe previous paragraphs mentions the advantages, and this one immediately introduces the downside, so the narrative is easy to trace.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-7-q42.explanation: BIt is easier to have a look at a paragraph that follows this one — it starts with “The writer …”, suggesting that the previous paragraph introduced a writer and possibly a book. Paragraph B is the only one fitting this description.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-7-q43.explanation: AThe preceding paragraphs numbers the downsides of the Internet in contrast with the advantages of more conventional reading from a book. Then this paragraph suggests that despite of all the downsides, the web offers best possibility for quick and efficient learning: “… a medium that would rewire our mental circuits as quickly and thoroughly as possible… “

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-7-q44.explanation: DThe paragraph before focuses on how a brain can me “malleable” — or able to change. Then Paragraph D continues and expands the idea by explaining and giving examples. The next paragraph starts with “When I ask him… “ it is clear that ‘he’ is Dr. Small.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-7-q45.explanation: FAt the very end of Paragraph F online games are mentioned. The paragraph that follows continues this idea with the example of Second Life virtual world type of game.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-7-q46.explanation: CThe game talk continues and Dr. Small explains how playing a game can be beneficial for your thinking: “you have to pay an incredible amount of attention to what your team-mates are doing, to the mechanics of the game”

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-8-q47.explanation: CThe ‘other’ factor here is label. The example illustrates how people can be mislead by a changed label on potato crisps.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-8-q48.explanation: BReaction to green can be both positive and negative — a ripe cucumber or an unripe fruit.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-8-q49.explanation: DThe example in the middle of Paragraph D talks about people with poor colour perception and how it affects their appetite.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-8-q50.explanation: AThe paragraph mentions two people who worked together to conduct an experiment in taste preference.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-8-q51.explanation: DThe bottom half of the paragraph talks about a man who sustained an injury that impaired his colour vision and it affected his food preferences dramatically.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-8-q52.explanation: A‘Food pictures masquerading as cookbooks’ is what the author meant here. This suggests that the original idea of cookbooks (to help cooking by giving recipes) is overlooked in favour of just gazing at highly-appetising pictures.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-8-q53.explanation: BThe blue and green meat examples are meant. Disgust = get sick.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-8-q54.explanation: DThe example with blind people shows how they are more capable of telling the slight differences in taste, compared to people with sight.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-8-q55.explanation: CExamples with Skittles and M&Ms — they colour each candy differently to subtly make us want to eat more of them.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test9-part-8-q56.explanation: BExample with green-dyed meat suggests that some would be unwilling to taste it: ‘your stomach probably turns.’
